Newly hatched Ambystoma texanum larvae emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably small size, with a total length at birth measuring approximately 1.0 cm [Lb = approximately 1.0 cm]. This diminutive size reflects the modest investment per offspring, as each larva begins life with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. The developing embryos within the jelly-coated eggs rely entirely on their yolk reserves, and the timing of hatching is strongly temperature-dependent. When eggs are incubated at a constant 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the age at birth averages 35 days [ab = 35 days], a duration that falls near the middle of the observed range of 29 to 82 days reported for this species under natural thermal regimes. The relatively long incubation period at this cool temperature is consistent with the decelerated developmental rates typical of many ambystomatid salamanders breeding in early spring, when ephemeral ponds remain cold and oxygen-rich. Following eclosion, the free-swimming larvae, still bearing a small yolk sac, begin a period of rapid exogenous feeding on aquatic microinvertebrates.

The larval period of Ambystoma texanum is characterized by sustained growth and morphological development, culminating in metamorphosis. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is 56 days , a value that aligns with the seven to nine week interval frequently cited for this species. At this developmental milestone, the recently metamorphosed juvenile typically attains a wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.59 grams , representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. This weight gain reflects the efficient conversion of consumed prey into somatic tissue during the aquatic larval phase. The transformation itself involves a dramatic body plan reorganization, including gill resorption, tail resorption, and skin keratinisation, which equips the animal for a terrestrial existence. Following recruitment to land, the juvenile salamanders enter a period of continued growth and foraging, gradually accumulating the energy reserves necessary to support future reproductive effort as they move toward sexual maturation.

Reproductive output in female Ambystoma texanum is tightly linked to body size, with larger individuals capable of producing more eggs. At a typical adult mass of 25.3 grams, females exhibit a daily reproduction rate that emerges from the combination of clutch size and breeding frequency. Field studies conducted at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] indicate that each female deposits between 350 and 900 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 350 and 900 eggs per clutch], and most individuals produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 15.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 15.7 grams], a value comparable to that reported for the congeneric species Ambystoma macrodactylum. This adult mass is attained after several years of post-metamorphic growth and represents the asymptotic body size under typical resource conditions. The trade-off between current reproductive investment and future survival appears to constrain females to a single annual breeding event, despite the potential physiological capacity for additional clutches.

Adult body size in Ambystoma texanum varies considerably across its geographic range, but the ultimate total length most commonly reported is around 19 centimeters [Li = around 19 centimeters]. While some individuals may exceed 23 centimeters, such large specimens are rare, and the species' typical maximum is considerably smaller than the 45 centimeters occasionally listed in general references. The ultimate wet weight for females of 15.7 grams [Wwi = 15.7 grams] corresponds to this modal adult length, reflecting the robust body proportions characteristic of this mole salamander. Maximum longevity in this species, recorded under controlled conditions maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], is approximately 5037 days [am = approximately 5037 days], which is equivalent to roughly 13.8 years. This lifespan is notable among ambystomatids and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace, with individuals investing in somatic maintenance over many seasons before eventual senescence and natural mortality occur.

Sexual maturation in Ambystoma texanum is a gradual process, with individuals typically attaining puberty well after completing metamorphosis and establishing themselves as terrestrial juveniles. The time since birth at puberty, measured under laboratory conditions at a stable 17 °C [T = 17 °C], is estimated at 548 days [tp = 548 days]. This interval represents approximately one and a half years of post-hatching development before the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis. The delay between metamorphosis and reproductive activation is likely an adaptive strategy, allowing young salamanders to accumulate sufficient body reserves and reach the critical body size necessary for successful first reproduction. By deferring reproductive investment until they have achieved an adequate mass and fat stores, individuals improve their prospects for producing a viable clutch. This pattern of delayed maturation aligns with the broader life history of the genus, where a trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth shapes the trajectory toward adulthood.
